key_facts: **Perioral dermatitis** is a facial eruption of tiny papules and pustules around the mouth, nose or eyes with **sparing next to the lips**.
Commonest in women aged 20–45 and children; often provoked by **topical, inhaled or nasal steroids** and heavy creams.
No comedones (unlike acne); no flushing (unlike rosacea).
Stop steroids and cosmetics, expect a rebound; topical metronidazole or azelaic acid; oral tetracycline for 6–8 weeks if needed.
Children under 12: erythromycin rather than tetracycline.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Perioral dermatitis** (periorificial dermatitis) is a common facial eruption of small papules and pustules around the mouth, nose and sometimes eyes, with a characteristic **clear zone next to the lip vermilion**. It mainly affects women aged 20–45 and children.

sub: Women 20–45 most; prepubertal children (often periocular, steroid-related).

ul: **Topical corticosteroids** on the face are the commonest trigger; also inhaled or nasal steroids, and heavy moisturisers or foundations.
Fluorinated toothpaste and barrier disruption may contribute.
Steroids disrupt the barrier and the follicle; occlusive cosmetics; possibly fluorinated toothpaste and microbiome changes.
**"Hydrocortisone will settle it"**: it masks it briefly and then makes it worse.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Steroids and occlusion damage the **barrier around facial follicles**, triggering inflammation.

mech.t: Steroids and heavy creams thin the barrier and alter the follicular microbiome.
Innate immune activation causes small papules and pustules around follicles.
Steroids suppress the rash; stopping causes rebound, so patients reapply.
mech.caption: Perioral dermatitis: papules around the mouth and nose, with a clear rim next to the lips.

mech.t: Stopping the trigger and anti-inflammatory treatment restores the barrier over weeks.

histo: Rarely needed: perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate; granulomatous in the granulomatous variant.

ul: Monomorphic 1–2 mm red papules, papulovesicles and pustules on a red, sometimes scaly background.
Around the mouth, nasolabial folds, chin; may involve the sides of the nose and eyelids (**periocular**).
**Vermilion sparing**: a narrow clear rim around the lips.
Burning or tightness more than itch; no comedones.

sub: Yellow-brown papules in children of African descent; slower to clear; refer if persistent.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Clinical. Ask specifically about steroid creams, inhalers, nasal sprays and cosmetics.

head: Look-alike
Clues
rows: Older; flushing; central face; no clear perioral rim
Greasy scale in nasolabial folds and brows
Itch, eczematous, linked to a product

ul: **Stop the facial steroid** (taper systemic or high-potency use with the prescriber; never stop inhaled asthma steroids: rinse and wipe the face after use).
Warn of a **rebound flare** for 1–2 weeks after stopping.
‘Zero therapy’: stop all creams and cosmetics; use a gentle cleanser only.
Oral tetracycline for 6–8 weeks if needed (erythromycin if under 12).

ladder.t: Stop facial steroids and heavy creams; gentle cleanser only.
Oral tetracycline 6–8 weeks if needed (erythromycin if under 12).

refer.t: Not responding after 8–12 weeks, granulomatous or periocular disease, diagnostic doubt.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Granulomatous or periocular disease not responding, or diagnostic doubt: dermatology.
Clears over 6–12 weeks with treatment; recurs if steroids are restarted.

pearls: Pharmacists often spot inhaled-steroid perioral dermatitis: advise rinsing and wiping the face after inhalers.
Hydrocortisone makes it look better briefly, then worse.

quiz.a: Topical (or inhaled/nasal) corticosteroids on the face.

quiz.q: What is the classic sign around the lips?
quiz.a: A clear rim next to the vermilion (vermilion sparing).

quiz.q: What happens after stopping the steroid?
